source: What Child Is This - We Voice (Part 1 of 2), Entry 12

blocks.text: 12: WHY ARE THERE TWO DIFFERENT FAMILY TREES FOR JESUS, AND WHY DOES THE DIFFERENCE MATTER MORE THAN THE SIMILARITY?

sentences: We touched on the two genealogies in Entry 5, establishing that Matthew and Luke were different authors writing for different audiences with different purposes, and that the three foundational facts they both get right, the virgin birth, the parents, and the Davidic descent, carry more evidentiary weight than the organizational differences that have led critics to call them contradictory.
That argument stands.
What Entry 5 didn't have space to do was develop the most important reason the two genealogies diverge after King David, because that reason isn't a discrepancy.
It's the most theologically precise detail in the entire Christmas story.
The divergence exists because there's a curse sitting in Matthew's genealogy, and Luke's genealogy is the only thing that gets around it.
In Jeremiah chapter twenty-two, the prophet records a divine declaration against a king named Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, who ruled Judah briefly before being carried into Babylonian exile.
The declaration is stark and specific: record this man as if childless, for none of his offspring will prosper, and none will sit on the throne of David or rule anymore in Judah.
This isn't a general statement about Jeconiah's personal misfortune.
It's a formal curse on his royal line, pronounced by God through the prophet Jeremiah, prohibiting any of Jeconiah's descendants from inheriting the Davidic throne.
The throne of David, the seat that the Messianic promise required the coming king to occupy, was closed to Jeconiah's biological line from that moment forward.
Now turn to Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.
In verse eleven of chapter one, Matthew lists Josiah as the father of Jeconiah.
Jeconiah is in the genealogy.
Jeconiah is in the direct line from David to Joseph.
Joseph the carpenter, the legal father of Jesus, is a biological descendant of Jeconiah.
This creates a problem that most readers of the Christmas story never encounter, because most readers of the Christmas story never read Jeremiah twenty-two alongside Matthew chapter one.
The problem is this: the Messiah must be from the line of David.
The promise in Second Samuel and confirmed through the prophets is unambiguous on this point.
The Messiah must also inherit the Davidic throne.
Jeremiah twenty-two says no biological descendant of Jeconiah can do that.
Joseph is a biological descendant of Jeconiah.
Any biological son of Joseph is barred from the throne by the curse.
Matthew includes Jeconiah in the genealogy and doesn't explain the problem.
He leaves it sitting there in verse eleven with no annotation.
A fabricator who understood the Jewish scriptures well enough to construct a Messianic lineage wouldn't create this problem for himself.
He would route the genealogy around Jeconiah entirely.
Matthew doesn't, because Matthew is recording the actual family line of Joseph, and the actual family line of Joseph runs through Jeconiah whether Matthew likes it or not.

blocks.text: THE SOLUTION THAT ONLY THE VIRGIN BIRTH PROVIDES

sentences: Luke's genealogy, tracing what the weight of evidence indicates is Mary's line, diverges from Matthew's at a precise and significant point.
Both genealogies agree that Jesus is descended from David.
Both run through David's family.
After David, they split.
Matthew's line goes through Solomon, David's son and successor to the throne, and continues through the royal Solomonic line all the way to Jeconiah and then to Joseph.
Luke's line goes through Nathan, another of David's sons, who never sat on the throne and whose line therefore never passed through Jeconiah.
The curse never touches Nathan's descendants.
Mary is a descendant of David through Nathan.
The curse of Jeconiah, running through Solomon's line, isn't in her genealogy at all.
Now the architecture of the solution becomes visible.
Jesus receives His legal right to the Davidic throne through Joseph, who's His legal father under the terms of the betrothal and adoption structure established in Hebrew marriage law.
Joseph is David's heir through the royal Solomonic line, the line with the strongest legal claim to the throne.
Jesus inherits that legal claim.
He's the legal son of Joseph, and through Joseph, the legal heir of David.
Jesus receives His biological descent from Mary, whose line runs through Nathan and bypasses Jeconiah entirely.
He's biologically a son of David without being biologically connected to the cursed line.
The curse applies to biological offspring of Jeconiah.
Jesus isn't a biological offspring of Jeconiah.
The curse doesn't touch Him.
The virgin birth is what makes this arrangement work.
If Jesus were the biological son of Joseph, He would be a biological descendant of Jeconiah, and Jeremiah twenty-two would bar Him from the throne regardless of His legal standing.
If Jesus had no legal connection to Joseph's line, He would lack the legal claim to the Solomonic royal succession.

The virgin birth is the only mechanism that simultaneously provides the legal inheritance through Joseph's line and the biological Davidic descent through Mary's line while keeping the Jeconiah curse out of His biological inheritance.
Three requirements.
One solution.
That solution is the virgin birth.
This is the argument the outline identified as one of the strongest Christmas-specific apologetic points in the source material, and it deserves to be stated directly.
No one engineering a forged Messianic genealogy arrives at this solution, because no one engineering a forged Messianic genealogy knows there's a problem that requires a solution.
The Jeconiah curse isn't a well-known fact of popular religious knowledge.
It requires a careful reader of Jeremiah twenty-two to notice, a careful comparison of the two genealogies to trace, and a sophisticated understanding of Hebrew inheritance law to fully appreciate.
The person who constructs a forgery to make Jesus look like the Messiah is constructing a narrative, not solving a genealogical puzzle embedded in prophetic literature from six centuries earlier.
The fact that the Christmas story not only contains this puzzle but resolves it with a precision that requires the virgin birth to work tells us something significant.

It tells us that the people involved in transmitting and recording this story understood the Jewish scriptures well enough to recognize a constraint they hadn't created, and that the account they were transmitting resolved that constraint in the only way it could be resolved.
The two family trees are different because they need to be different.
The difference isn't a problem in the Christmas story.
It's the solution to one.
Matthew includes Jeconiah in the genealogy of Jesus without explaining the problem the Jeconiah curse creates for any biological descendant of Joseph who wants to claim the Davidic throne.

Why would a writer constructing a favorable narrative about Jesus include a detail that creates a significant theological problem without offering any resolution to that problem within the same document?

The virgin birth resolves three simultaneous requirements: legal Davidic descent through Joseph, biological Davidic descent through Mary, and exemption from the Jeconiah curse through Mary's Nathan line.

If the virgin birth were invented as a miracle story with no genealogical function, why would it happen to resolve a constraint embedded in Jeremiah twenty-two that most readers of the Christmas story never encounter?

The Jeconiah problem requires knowledge of Jeremiah twenty-two, careful comparison of two genealogies in two different gospels, and an understanding of how Hebrew inheritance law distinguished legal from biological paternity.
What does it tell us about the Christmas story that it contains a problem this specific, and a solution this precise, in what most people treat as a list of names to skip?
